chapters.name: Chapter 1: Reading science and understanding experiments

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How the GED Science test works
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the parts and tools of the GED Science test and write a study plan with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official GED website, you will list the parts, question types, time and tools of the GED Science test and write a study plan with dates, with all three skill areas named and at least one study date each week until the test.
The GED has four tests: Math, Reasoning Through Language Arts, Science and Social Studies. You can take them one at a time. The GED Testing Service makes the test. Some states use another high school equivalency test, HiSET, so check which test your state uses.
On ged.com, the Science test is listed as 90 minutes with no break. It covers three skill areas: reading for meaning in science, designing and interpreting science experiments, and using numbers and graphics in science. Questions are multiple choice, fill in the blank, drag and drop, select an area and drop-down.
You get an on-screen calculator and a calculator reference sheet, and ged.com says you may bring your own TI-30XS calculator to a test center. Ged.com also says you do not need to memorize formulas: the information you need is given with each question. It is not a test of memorized facts; it tests how you read and reason.
Ged.com lists a passing score of 145 for each subject. Times and rules can change, so check ged.com before you book. Ged.com has free sample tests and an official practice test, GED Ready.
Step by step:
- Go to ged.com and read the Science test page.
- Write down the time, the three skill areas and the tools you get.
- Take the free sample Science test to see where you stand.
- Pick a target test week.
- Write at least one study date each week, with the skill you will practice.
Words to know:
- GED: a high school equivalency test; passing all four subjects earns a credential that many employers and colleges accept like a diploma.
- HiSET: another high school equivalency test that some states use.
- TI-30XS: the model of hand calculator the GED test uses on screen and allows at test centers.
- Calculator reference sheet: a sheet given on the test that shows how to use the calculator's keys.
Official sources:
- GED Testing Service: test subjects (time, question types, calculator)
- GED Testing Service: Science test
- GED Testing Service: scores
- GED Testing Service: free sample tests (English and Spanish)
- GED Ready, the official practice test
- HiSET, another high school equivalency test (official site)
Try it now: Open ged.com and take the free Science sample test (or read the Science page if you cannot take it now). Write your study plan: your target test week and one date each week with the skill you will practice: reading science, experiments, or numbers and graphs. Keep it for the final task.
You can now name the parts and tools of the GED Science test and follow a study plan with dates.

check.q: According to ged.com, what do you need to memorize for the GED Science test?
options: Not formulas: the information you need is given with each question
check.why: Ged.com says you do not need to memorize formulas; the needed information is provided.

check.q: Which is one of the three skill areas of the Science test?
check.why: Ged.com lists reading for meaning, experiments, and numbers and graphics.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading a science passage
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the main idea of a science passage and the claim its evidence supports.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short science passage, you will identify the main idea and the claim that the passage's evidence supports, pointing to the sentence or number that supports each answer.
Science passages look hard because of new words, but you read them the same way as any passage. Find what it is mostly about, and find the facts and numbers that back it up. Often the passage explains a hard word right in the text. Look for "is called", "means" or a word in commas after it.
Worked example. "Sweat cools the body. When sweat evaporates, or turns from liquid into gas, it takes heat away from the skin. On humid days, the air already holds a lot of water, so sweat evaporates more slowly." Main idea: sweating cools the body by evaporation. Supported claim: you may feel hotter on humid days because sweat dries more slowly.
A claim is supported only if the passage gives evidence for it. "Sweating burns fat" is not supported; the passage says nothing about fat. Pick the answer that the text proves, not the one that sounds most scientific.
Step by step:
- Read the question first.
- Read the passage; circle new words and look for their meaning nearby.
- Say the main idea in one sentence.
- For each answer choice, ask: where does the passage prove this?
- Cross out choices that add facts the passage does not give.
Words to know:
- Evaporate: to change from a liquid into a gas, like a puddle drying up.
- Humid: when the air holds a lot of water vapor.
- Claim: a statement that something is true.
- Supported: backed up by evidence in the text or data.
Try it now: Practice passage: "Plants make their own food through photosynthesis. They use light, water and carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, to make sugar. They release oxygen as a result." 1) Main idea? 2) Which claim is supported: (a) a plant kept in a dark closet will have trouble making food, or (b) plants need soda to grow? Answers: 1) Plants make food from light, water and carbon dioxide. 2) (a): the passage says plants need light. (b) is not in the text.
You can now find the main idea of a science passage and pick the claim its evidence supports.

check.q: A passage says, "Vaccines train the immune system, the body's defense system, to recognize germs." What does "immune system" mean here?
options: A type of medicine you swallow
check.why: The meaning is given in the commas right after the word.

check.q: A passage says steel rusts faster in wet, salty air. Which claim is supported?
options: A steel bridge near the ocean may need more rust protection
check.why: Ocean air is wet and salty, and the passage says that speeds up rust.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Experiments: hypothesis and variables
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name the hypothesis and the independent, dependent and controlled variables in an experiment.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of an experiment, you will name the hypothesis and the independent, dependent and controlled variables, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
An experiment tests a question. The hypothesis is a testable guess about the answer, often written "If ..., then ...". For example: "If plants get more hours of light, then they will grow taller."
The independent variable is the one thing the scientist changes on purpose (hours of light). The dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect (plant height). Controlled variables are kept the same so the test is fair (same kind of plant, same pot, same water, same soil).
A trick to remember: the dependent variable depends on the independent one. Height depends on light. A fair test changes only one thing at a time. If you change light and water together, you cannot tell which one made the plant grow.
Good experiments repeat each trial several times and often have a control group, a group that gets no change, to compare against. More trials make the results more reliable.
Step by step:
- Find the question being tested.
- Find the one thing changed on purpose: the independent variable.
- Find what is measured: the dependent variable.
- List what is kept the same: the controlled variables.
- Check only one thing changes, and that trials are repeated.
Words to know:
- Hypothesis: a testable guess, often "If ..., then ...".
- Independent variable: the one thing you change on purpose.
- Dependent variable: what you measure to see the effect.
- Controlled variable: something you keep the same so the test is fair.
- Control group: a group that gets no change, used for comparison.
Try it now: Practice: A worker tests whether a new glove keeps hands warmer. Ten workers wear the new glove and ten wear the old glove, outside for 30 minutes at the same time. Hand temperature is measured. Name: 1) independent variable, 2) dependent variable, 3) two controlled variables, 4) a hypothesis. Answers: 1) type of glove; 2) hand temperature; 3) time outside, same weather, same time of day; 4) "If workers wear the new glove, then their hands will be warmer."
You can now read an experiment and name its hypothesis and its variables, and spot an unfair test.

check.q: A student tests if salt changes how fast ice melts. What is the dependent variable?
options: The size of the ice cubes
The time it takes the ice to melt
check.why: Melting time is what is measured; it depends on the salt.

check.q: Why should an experiment change only one thing at a time?
options: So you know which change caused the result
check.why: If two things change, you cannot tell which one made the difference.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Numbers, tables and graphs in science

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading tables and graphs
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read values from a table or graph, describe the trend and pick the conclusion the data supports.
This lesson builds toward: Given a table or a graph, you will read values, describe the trend and choose the conclusion the data supports, without adding facts that are not in the data.
Many science questions give you a table or a graph. First read the title, the labels and the units. On a graph, the label on the bottom (x-axis) is usually the independent variable, and the label on the side (y-axis) is the dependent variable.
Worked example. Table: "Hours of light per day: 4, 8, 12. Average plant height after 3 weeks: 5 cm, 9 cm, 14 cm." Read a value: at 8 hours, plants grew 9 cm. Trend: as light goes up, height goes up. Supported conclusion: in this test, more light went with taller plants.
Do not go past the data. The table does not show 20 hours of light, so you cannot say what happens then. It also does not show water or soil, so a conclusion about them is not supported.
Graph types: a bar graph compares groups, a line graph shows change over time or a trend, and a pie chart shows parts of a whole.
Step by step:
- Read the title, labels and units.
- Find the value the question asks about.
- Describe the trend: up, down, or no clear pattern.
- Choose the conclusion that stays inside the data.
- Cross out answers about things the data does not show.
Words to know:
- Trend: the general direction of data: going up, going down or staying flat.
- X-axis: the line across the bottom of a graph.
- Y-axis: the line up the side of a graph.
- Units: what a number is measured in, like cm, degrees or minutes.
Try it now: Practice table: "Water temperature (degrees C): 10, 20, 30, 40. Time for a sugar cube to dissolve (seconds): 120, 90, 60, 40." 1) How long at 30 degrees? 2) What is the trend? 3) Which conclusion is supported: (a) warmer water dissolved sugar faster in this test, or (b) salt dissolves faster than sugar? Answers: 1) 60 seconds. 2) As temperature goes up, dissolving time goes down. 3) (a); salt was not tested.
You can now read a table or graph, describe its trend, and choose a conclusion the data supports.

check.q: A graph shows a town's average temperature rising each decade from 1980 to 2020. What is the trend?
check.why: The values go up across the decades.

check.q: A table shows plant height for 4, 8 and 12 hours of light. Which conclusion goes beyond the data?
options: Plants with 8 hours grew taller than plants with 4
Plants given 24 hours of light will be the tallest
Height went up as light went up
Plants with 12 hours grew the most in this test
check.why: 24 hours was not tested, so the data cannot tell you that.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Science math: averages, range and formulas
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a data set and use a given formula.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small set of data or a formula, you will calculate the mean, median, mode and range or use the formula to find an answer, with the right units and getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Data set (practice only): heart rates after a walk, in beats per minute: 80, 84, 84, 90, 92. Mean (average): add them and divide by how many: 430 / 5 = 86. Median: the middle number when they are in order: 84. Mode: the number that appears most: 84. Range: largest minus smallest: 92 - 80 = 12.
If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle numbers. For 3, 5, 7, 9: (5 + 7) / 2 = 6.
Formulas are given on the test. Plug in the numbers and keep the units. Speed = distance / time: a truck goes 120 miles in 2 hours, so speed = 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour. Density = mass / volume: a block of 40 grams with a volume of 20 cubic centimeters has density 40 / 20 = 2 grams per cubic centimeter.
Check that your answer makes sense. A mean must be between the smallest and largest values. Write the unit with every answer.
Step by step:
- Put the data in order from smallest to largest.
- Mean: add all values and divide by how many.
- Median: find the middle (or the average of the two middle values).
- Mode: the most common value. Range: largest minus smallest.
- For a formula: write it, plug in numbers, solve, and add the units.
Words to know:
- Mean: the average: the total divided by how many values.
- Median: the middle value when numbers are in order.
- Mode: the value that appears most often.
- Range: the largest value minus the smallest.
- Density: how much mass is packed into a space: mass divided by volume.
Try it now: Practice only. 1) Minutes for an ice cube to melt in five trials: 6, 7, 7, 8, 12. Find the mean, median, mode and range. 2) A cyclist rides 30 miles in 3 hours. Speed = distance / time. Answers: 1) Mean 40 / 5 = 8 minutes; median 7; mode 7; range 12 - 6 = 6 minutes. 2) 30 / 3 = 10 miles per hour.
You can now find the mean, median, mode and range of data and use a science formula with the right units.

check.q: A rock has mass 60 grams and volume 20 cubic centimeters. Density = mass / volume. What is the density?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Putting it together: your own fair test
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a fair test, record data in a table, find the mean and write a conclusion the data supports.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of an experiment, you will name the hypothesis and the independent, dependent and controlled variables, getting at least 4 of 5 right. Given a table or a graph, you will read values, describe the trend and choose the conclusion the data supports, without adding facts that are not in the data. Given a small set of data or a formula, you will calculate the mean, median, mode and range or use the formula to find an answer, with the right units and getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Now use every skill at once. Many test questions describe a whole experiment with a table, then ask about the variables, the math and the conclusion. Doing a small experiment yourself makes these questions much easier.
Safe kitchen example. Question: does stirring change how fast sugar dissolves? Hypothesis: if the water is stirred, then the sugar will dissolve faster. Independent variable: stirred or not stirred. Dependent variable: time to dissolve (seconds). Controlled: same cup, same amount of tap water, same water temperature, one sugar cube each time. Do three trials of each.
Sample results (practice only). Stirred: 40, 45, 50 seconds; mean 45. Not stirred: 170, 180, 190 seconds; mean 180. Conclusion: in this test, stirring made sugar dissolve faster, about 4 times faster on average. A bar graph with two bars (stirred, not stirred) shows this clearly.
Safety: use only tap water at room temperature or warm from the tap, sugar or salt, and clean cups. No stove, no flames and no cleaning chemicals. Do not drink or taste anything during the test.
Step by step:
- Write your question and an "If ..., then ..." hypothesis.
- Name the independent, dependent and controlled variables.
- Run at least three trials of each group and write the results in a table.
- Find the mean for each group.
- Sketch a bar graph and write a two-sentence conclusion that stays inside your data.
Words to know:
- Trial: one run of an experiment.
- Data table: rows and columns that hold your results.
- Conclusion: what the results show, in a sentence or two.
Try it now: Final task: run your own small, safe kitchen experiment (stirring and sugar, or another one-change test with water, sugar or salt). Write the question, hypothesis and variables, record three trials per group in a table, find each mean, sketch a bar graph and write a two-sentence conclusion. Add your dated GED study plan at the bottom and score it with the rubric.
You can now plan and run a fair test, record and average the data, and write a conclusion that the data supports.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Question and hypothesis No question, or the hypothesis cannot be tested. A clear question and an "If ..., then ..." hypothesis. The hypothesis also says why the writer expects that result. Variables and fair test Variables are missing or more than one thing changes. Independent, dependent and at least two controlled variables are named; only one thing changes. Also includes a control group and explains why each controlled variable matters. Data and math Fewer than three trials per group, or the mean is wrong. Three trials per group in a table, with a correct mean and units. Also gives the range for each group and comments on how much the trials varied. Graph and conclusion No graph, or the conclusion claims more than the data shows. A labeled bar graph and a two-sentence conclusion that stays inside the data. Also names one way to improve the test next time. Reading the results The conclusion does not match the numbers. The conclusion matches the numbers in the table. Points to the exact numbers that support the conclusion. Study plan No study plan, or no dates. A study plan with at least one date each week through the target test week. Also includes a date for GED Ready or a booked test date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and run the test again.

check.q: In the stirring test, which must stay the same for a fair test?
options: The amount and temperature of the water
check.why: Water amount and temperature are controlled variables; only stirring changes.

check.q: Stirred mean: 45 seconds. Not stirred mean: 180 seconds. Which conclusion is supported?
options: In this test, stirring made sugar dissolve faster
check.why: The stirred cups dissolved much faster, and the conclusion stays inside the data.
